name: Silk
economic_significance: Luxury textile that drove transcontinental trade; basis of the Silk Road economy

name: Black Pepper
economic_significance: Called "black gold"; most traded spice in history; drove European Age of Exploration

name: Cinnamon
economic_significance: One of the earliest traded spices; highly valued in ancient Egypt and Rome

name: Clove
economic_significance: Extremely valuable spice monopolized by successive colonial powers

name: Nutmeg
economic_significance: Once worth more than gold by weight; cause of colonial wars over Banda Islands

name: Gold
economic_significance: Universal store of value; primary driver of trans-Saharan and colonial trade

name: Silver
economic_significance: Primary currency metal; Spanish silver from Americas transformed global economy

name: Tin
economic_significance: Essential for bronze production; scarcity drove long-distance trade networks

name: Copper
economic_significance: Foundation of Bronze Age economy; Cyprus named for copper (cuprum)

name: Amber
economic_significance: Precious resin traded from Baltic to Mediterranean; defined the Amber Road

name: Frankincense
economic_significance: Sacred resin central to religious rituals across civilizations; drove Arabian wealth

name: Myrrh
economic_significance: Aromatic resin used in medicine, embalming, and religious ceremonies

name: Ivory
economic_significance: High-value luxury material; trade linked closely to slave trade routes

name: Salt
economic_significance: Essential commodity; "worth its weight in gold" in sub-Saharan Africa

name: Tea
economic_significance: World's most consumed beverage after water; drove British colonial expansion

name: Coffee
economic_significance: Transformed social culture globally; second most traded commodity after oil

name: Sugar
economic_significance: White gold that drove plantation slavery and reshaped demographics of Americas

name: Cotton
economic_significance: Revolutionized textile industry; cotton trade linked to slavery and industrialization

name: Wool
economic_significance: Staple textile of temperate civilizations; English wool trade built medieval economy

name: Horses
economic_significance: Revolutionized warfare and transport; Mongol Empire built on horse mastery

name: Porcelain
economic_significance: White gold of trade; Chinese monopoly for centuries shaped global commerce

name: Obsidian
economic_significance: Earliest long-distance traded commodity; volcanic glass prized for tools and weapons

name: Lapis Lazuli
economic_significance: Prized blue stone traded across ancient world; source of ultramarine pigment

name: Jade
economic_significance: Sacred stone in Chinese and Mesoamerican cultures; "stone of heaven"

name: Incense
economic_significance: Sacred aromatic resins essential to religious practices across civilizations

name: Spice Mix (Garam Masala)
economic_significance: Complex spice blends that defined Indian cuisine and drove spice trade

name: Indigo
economic_significance: Most important natural dye; Indian indigo monopoly drove colonial plantation systems

name: Sandalwood
economic_significance: Fragrant wood prized for incense, medicine, and carving across Asia

name: Camphor
economic_significance: Aromatic compound highly valued in Chinese and Islamic medicine

name: Slaves
economic_significance: Forced human labor trade that shaped demographics, economies, and cultures globally

name: Furs
economic_significance: Luxury pelts that drove Russian expansion into Siberia and French/British colonization of North America

name: Gems (Rubies)
economic_significance: Precious gemstones traded across Asia; Myanmar rubies the most prized

name: Iron
economic_significance: Revolutionary metal that transformed warfare and agriculture; defined an age

name: Rice
economic_significance: Staple food for half of humanity; rice paddy culture shaped Asian civilizations

name: Papyrus
economic_significance: Writing material that enabled record-keeping; Egyptian monopoly for millennia

name: Wine
economic_significance: Cultural beverage central to Mediterranean civilizations; Phoenicians spread viticulture

name: Cowrie Shells
economic_significance: Universal currency across Africa and Asia; most widely used shell money in history

name: Opium
economic_significance: Medicinal and recreational drug; opium trade triggered wars and shaped colonial politics

name: Rubber
economic_significance: Essential industrial material; rubber boom reshaped Amazon region and Congo

name: Tobacco
economic_significance: New World crop that became globally addictive; tobacco trade drove colonial economies

name: Cocoa
economic_significance: Sacred Mesoamerican crop; chocolate became luxury European commodity

name: Diamonds
economic_significance: Hardest natural substance; Indian diamond trade ancient, South African diamonds transformed global market

name: Turmeric
economic_significance: Golden spice with culinary, medicinal, and ceremonial uses; staple of Indian trade

name: Saffron
economic_significance: Most expensive spice by weight; labor-intensive harvest from crocus flowers

name: Pearls
economic_significance: Prized oceanic gems; Persian Gulf pearl diving sustained Arabian Gulf economies for millennia

name: Textiles
economic_significance: Aggregate category for woven cloth traded as a commodity where the sources name no single fibre — Levantine and Anatolian weaves on the Persian Royal Road, Andean camelid cloth on the Inca road system, European broadcloth on the Camino Real

name: Grain
origin_region: Fertile Crescent and the Nile Valley
economic_significance: Wheat and barley, the staple bulk cargo of Mediterranean and Near Eastern trade; Egyptian and Black Sea grain fed Rome and Constantinople

name: Spices
economic_significance: Aggregate category for mixed spice cargoes where the sources name no single spice; anchored on the Malabar Coast, the dominant entrepot for the assorted-spice trade

name: Metal Ores
economic_significance: Aggregate category for unworked copper, tin, lead and iron ore moved in bulk; anchored on Cyprus, whose copper named the metal

name: Metalwork
economic_significance: Aggregate category for finished metal goods — weapons, tools, vessels and ornament — distinct from raw ore; anchored on Damascus, long synonymous with high-value worked steel

name: Cedar
economic_significance: Rot-resistant timber from the Lebanese highlands, exported through Byblos for Egyptian and Mesopotamian temple, palace and ship construction; one of the earliest documented long-distance bulk trades

name: Marble
economic_significance: Monumental building and sculptural stone; Pentelic marble built classical Athens and Carrara marble supplied Rome, moved by sea and along the Appian Way

name: Olive Oil
economic_significance: Cooking fat, lamp fuel, cosmetic and ritual unguent shipped in amphorae throughout the classical Mediterranean; one of the highest-volume Roman cargoes

name: Livestock
economic_significance: Cattle, sheep, mules and horses driven along overland routes as self-transporting cargo; the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro stocked the New Mexican frontier this way

name: Hides
economic_significance: Untanned skins and worked leather, a durable high-value-per-weight by-product of the livestock trade; a staple return cargo on the Camino Real and the Rus river routes

name: Maize
economic_significance: Domesticated in southern Mexico and the staple grain of Mesoamerica and the Andes; carried on the Inca road system as state-stored tribute and later spread worldwide by the Columbian exchange

name: Coca
economic_significance: Stimulant leaf chewed against altitude, hunger and fatigue; a ritual and labour good distributed along the Qhapaq Nan under Inca state control

name: Lacquerware
economic_significance: Sap-lacquered wood vessels and boxes, light, waterproof and highly durable; a premium East Asian export carried on the Nakasendo and later prized in Europe

name: Seafood
origin_region: Coastal Japan and the North Atlantic
economic_significance: Dried, salted and pickled fish and shellfish — a preserved protein cargo that could travel inland; fresh and dried seafood moved from Suruga Bay along the Tokaido to Edo
